lead: A continuous-time LTI system is causal when its output never depends on future input. It is bounded-input bounded-output (BIBO) stable when every bounded input gives a bounded output. For an LTI system both tests reduce to one signal: the impulse response h(t), the output to δ(t). Causality asks where h(t) is zero; stability asks whether the area under |h(t)| is finite. Engineers use these tests on filters, sensors and control loops before trusting a design.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for h(t), and Unit 1 system properties for the words causal and stable.

blocks.text: A system is causal if y(t) uses only present and past input, never future input. For an LTI system, y(t)=∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ. If h(t−τ) is nonzero for τ>t, future input reaches y(t). So the test is h(t)=0 for t<0. The response must start at t=0 or later. At t=0, h(0) may be nonzero; only negative time is banned.

blocks.where: h(t) is the impulse response; t is time.

blocks.text: For example, e^{−2t}u(t) is causal, while u(t+1) is not. A causal h(t) can still have infinite area, as u(t) shows. Shift a noncausal h to the right and it can become causal; shift a causal h left and it can become noncausal. The test uses only where h(t) sits in time, not its size. A real-time filter cannot use a response that reacts before the impulse arrives.

BIBO stable means every bounded input gives a bounded output. Let |x(t)|≤M_x<∞ and y(t)=∫h(τ)x(t−τ)dτ. Then |y(t)|≤M_x∫|h(τ)|dτ. A finite integral guarantees stability. The converse also holds: if the integral is infinite, some bounded input makes y(t) unbounded.

blocks.where: h(t) is the impulse response; |h(t)| is its absolute value; dt is a small time interval; the integral runs over all time.

blocks.text: This is the area under |h(t)|, called the L1 norm. Use absolute value; without it, positive and negative parts cancel and hide instability. For e^{−2t}u(t), area=∫_0^∞e^{−2t}dt=1/2, stable. For u(t), area=∫_0^∞1dt=∞, unstable. The input bound M_x is any finite number in the signal's units. The output bound M_y=M_x∫|h|dτ is finite when the area is finite. The units of ∫|h|dτ are seconds if h is dimensionless.

Causality and stability are independent. Causal does not imply stable: u(t) is zero for t<0 but has infinite area, so it is unstable. Stable does not imply causal: e^{2t}u(−t) has area 1/2 but is nonzero for t<0. Both can hold: e^{−2t}u(t). Neither can hold: e^{−t}u(−t) is nonzero for t<0 and its area is infinite. Only a few universities teach this as a separate chapter; most attach the tests to convolution.

In an exam, run them one after the other. First check h(t) for t<0. Then integrate |h(t)| over all time. Do not infer one property from the other. A causal system can be unstable, and a stable system can be noncausal. The tests answer different questions: when does h(t) start, and how much total absolute area does it contain?

figure.caption: The flowchart reads h(t) twice: negative-time values settle causality, then the absolute area settles BIBO stability. Both answers are needed; one does not imply the other.

examples.question: Test h₁(t)=e^{−2t}u(t), h₂(t)=e^{2t}u(−t), and h₃(t)=u(t) for causality and BIBO stability. Compute the finite areas under |h(t)|.
steps: h₁ is zero for t<0, so causal. Area=∫_0^∞e^{−2t}dt=[−e^{−2t}/2]_0^∞=1/2. Finite, so stable.
h₂ is nonzero for t<0, so not causal. Area=∫_{−∞}^0e^{2t}dt=[e^{2t}/2]_{−∞}^0=1/2. Finite, so stable.
h₃ is zero for t<0, so causal. Area=∫_0^∞1dt=∞, so not stable.
examples.answer: h₁ is causal and stable with area 0.5; h₂ is stable but not causal with area 0.5; h₃ is causal but not stable.
examples.check:
def area(a):
    return 1 / a
h1_area = area(2)
h2_area = area(2)
print(h1_area)
print(h2_area)

traps: Causal does not imply stable: u(t) is zero for t<0 but has infinite area, so it is unstable.
Stable does not imply causal: e^{2t}u(−t) has finite area 1/2 but is nonzero before t=0.
The stability integral must use |h(t)|; without absolute value, cancellation can make an unstable system look finite.
h(0) may be nonzero; causality only forbids t<0. Do not move the boundary to t≤0.
BIBO is a system property; test h(t), not one chosen input x(t).

quiz.q: State the causality condition on h(t) for a CT LTI system.
State the BIBO stability condition on h(t).
Why is u(t) causal but not BIBO stable?
quiz.a: u(t)=0 for t<0, so causal; ∫_0^∞1dt=∞, so unstable.

quiz.q: For h(t)=3e^{−4t}u(t), find causality and the area under |h(t)|.
quiz.a: h=0 for t<0, causal; area=3∫_0^∞e^{−4t}dt=3/4=0.75, stable.

quiz.q: For h(t)=e^{3t}u(−t), find causality and the area under |h(t)|.
quiz.a: Nonzero for t<0, not causal; area=∫_{−∞}^0e^{3t}dt=1/3≈0.333, stable.

quiz.q: For h(t)=e^{−t}u(t)+2e^{2t}u(−t), test causality and stability and give the area.
quiz.a: Second term is nonzero for t<0, so not causal. Area=1+2(1/2)=2, finite, stable.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, BIBO stability is checked with Laplace poles, and in sampled systems with z-plane poles; see Unit 4. The same impulse-response area bounds worst-case error in control and filter design. Search next for BIBO stability, L1 norm of impulse response, and absolute summability for discrete-time systems.
